receipts.first_text_witness: In 1904, Japan's first female journalist invented a budgeting system that people still buy unchanged in bookstores today. No app, no algorithm, just paper, a pen, and four questions. It's called Kakeibo.
receipts.last_text_witness: You need a few minutes a day, a savings goal you actually write down, and the habit of asking yourself once a month how you can improve. That's the whole thing. If this video made something click, subscribe and hit the like button. It tells the algorithm this is worth spreading, and if you want to see what happens when you take those savings and actually put them to work, the video on compound interest is right here. I'll see you there.

primary_source_receipts.claim: Motoko Hani's profession and magazine chronology
primary_source_receipts.finding: The National Diet Library says Hani joined Hochi-sha and became Japan's first woman journalist; she and Hani Yoshikazu began Katei no Tomo in 1903. This supports the identity and publication context but not every exact claim about the 1904 ledger form.

The high-density EEG experiment involved 36 university students and found more elaborate connectivity during stylus handwriting than one-finger typing. It did not test budgeting, savings or app abandonment.

The review synthesized 445 effects from 86 studies and estimated a 0.40 generation-over-reading benefit with substantial moderator variation. It did not study manually logged purchases or financial behavior.

A direct replication and mini meta-analyses did not support a reliable immediate-learning advantage from longhand note-taking through better encoding. The transcript's 'consistently outperformed' language is too categorical.

The university says 267 participants were recruited. More than 70% in the group sending weekly updates to a friend reported success versus 35% who kept goals private without writing; writing, commitments and accountability are confounded, so the comparison does not isolate writing.

The New York Fed report is the latest quarter available before the 2026-03-01 upload. Aggregate balances are descriptive and cannot establish that budgeting apps caused or failed to prevent debt. Later Q1/Q2 2026 values postdate publication.

Adjust reports a 9% global median day-30 retention rate for finance apps in 2023. It is not a budgeting-app-only result and does not reproduce the script's full 4-9% range or 84% annual abandonment claim.

calculation_receipts.assumptions: Frozen views and age_days; exact listed same-channel long-form peers under build_baseline.compare; first five listed peers for sensitivity.
A source supports only its measured population, intervention and outcome; transfer from learning/memory experiments to household saving requires separate evidence.
